# Problem 1: Vectorization

The following functions can be written to be more efficient without using parallelization. Write a faster version of each function and show that (1) the outputs are the same as the slow version, and (2) your version is faster.

## This function generates an n x k dataset with all its entries drawn from a Poission distribution with mean lambda. 

```{r}
fun1 <- function(n = 100, k = 4, lambda = 4) {
  x <- NULL
  
  for (i in 1:n){
    x <- rbind(x, rpois(k, lambda))    
  }
  
  return(x)
}

dim(fun1(100))
summary(fun1(100))
mean(fun1(100))

# Show that fun1alt generates a matrix with the same dimensions as fun1 and that the values inside the two matrices follow similar distributions. 

fun1alt <- function(n = 100, k = 4, lambda = 4) {
  matrix(rpois(n*k, lambda), nrow = n)
}
dim(fun1alt(100))
summary(fun1alt(100))
mean(fun1(100))

# Then check the speed of the two functions with the following code:
microbenchmark::microbenchmark(
  fun1(100),
  fun1alt(100)
)
```

### Summary

Both fun1 and fun1alt generate a 100 x 4 matrix and contain similar distributions of values. fun1alt is the faster function.

## This function finds the maximum value of each column of a matrix.

```{r}
# Data Generating Process (10 x 10,000 matrix)

# Show that both functions return the same output for a given input matrix, x. Then check the speed of the two functions, as you did above.

set.seed(1234)
x <- matrix(rnorm(1e4), nrow=10)

# Find each column's max value
fun2 <- function(x) {
  apply(x, 2, max)
}

fun2alt <- function(x) {
  do.call(pmax, unname(split(x,row(x))))
}

head(fun2(x), 10)
head(fun2alt(x), 10)
identical(fun2(x),fun2alt(x))

microbenchmark::microbenchmark(fun2(x), fun2alt(x))
```

### Summary

Both fun2 and fun2alt return the same output for the given input matrix x. fun2alt is the faster function.

# Problem 2: Parallelization

The main assumption is that we can approximate the results of many repeated experiments by resampling observations from our original dataset, which reflects the population.

## This function implements a serial version of the bootstrap. Edit this function to parallelize the lapply loop, using whichever method you prefer. Rather than specifying the number of cores to use, use the number given by the ncpus argument, so that we can test it with different numbers of cores later.

```{r}
my_boot <- function(dat, stat, R, ncpus = 1L) {
  
  # Getting the random indices
  n <- nrow(dat)
  idx <- matrix(sample.int(n, n*R, TRUE), nrow=n, ncol=R)
  
  cl <- makeCluster(ncpus)
  on.exit(stopCluster(cl))
  
  # THIS FUNCTION NEEDS TO BE PARALELLIZED
  # EDIT THIS CODE:
  
  ans <- parLapply(cl, seq_len(R), function(i, dat, idx, stat) {stat(dat[idx[,i], , drop = FALSE])}, dat = dat, idx = idx, stat = stat)

  # Converting the list into a matrix
  ans <- do.call(rbind, ans)

  return(ans)
}


```

## Once you have a version of the my_boot() function that runs on multiple cores, check that it provides accurate results by comparing it to a parametric model:

```{r}
# Bootstrap of an OLS
my_stat <- function(d) coef(lm(y ~ x, data=d))

# DATA SIM
set.seed(1)
n <- 500; R <- 1e4

x <- cbind(rnorm(n)); y <- x*5 + rnorm(n)

# Checking if we get something similar as lm
ans0 <- confint(lm(y~x))
ans1 <- my_boot(dat = data.frame(x, y), my_stat, R = R, ncpus = 2L)

# You should get something like this
t(apply(ans1, 2, quantile, c(.025,.975)))
##                   2.5%      97.5%
## (Intercept) -0.1372435 0.05074397
## x            4.8680977 5.04539763
ans0
##                  2.5 %     97.5 %
## (Intercept) -0.1379033 0.04797344
## x            4.8650100 5.04883353
```

## Check whether your version actually goes faster when it’s run on multiple cores (since this might take a little while to run, we’ll use system.time and just run each version once, rather than microbenchmark, which would run each version 100 times, by default):

```{r}
system.time(my_boot(dat = data.frame(x, y), my_stat, R = 4000, ncpus = 1L))
system.time(my_boot(dat = data.frame(x, y), my_stat, R = 4000, ncpus = 2L))
```

### Summary

The version running on two cores was faster than running on one core.
